query: For transition-metal catalysts, formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Altering the support’s electronic character to increase electron donation to identical transition‐metal nanoparticles shifts the d‐band center upward, thereby strengthening the adsorption of reaction intermediates and enhancing catalytic activity relative to catalysts on electronically neutral supports.
generation.material_initial_state: Transition‐metal nanoparticles (e.g., Pt‐based alloy) uniformly deposited on a support with no engineered electron-donating or -withdrawing modifications.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of catalysts by depositing the same metal nanoparticles on supports that have been modified: one set on supports engineered to be electron-donating and a baseline set on electronically neutral supports.
generation.conditions: Catalytic reactions performed under identical laboratory conditions (constant temperature, pressure, reactant concentrations) with identical nanoparticle size, composition, and morphology so that the only variable is the support’s electronic property.
generation.structural_mediator: Support-induced modulation of the active sites’ d-band center
generation.mechanism: Enhanced electron donation from the modified support increases the electron density at the metal active sites, shifting the d-band center upward. This electronic shift optimizes the adsorption/desorption balance of key reaction intermediates, such that binding becomes stronger and more favorable for catalysis, thereby increasing turnover frequency.
generation.predicted_outcome: Catalysts on electron-donating supports will show higher turnover frequencies and improved conversion rates compared to those on neutral supports when all other conditions are held constant.
generation.baseline: Catalysts with the same transition-metal nanoparticles deposited on electronically neutral supports.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under well-controlled laboratory conditions, particularly for reactions where adsorbate binding energetics are critical to reaction kinetics. It applies when nanoparticle size, composition, and geometric factors are strictly maintained and the only variable is the support’s capability for electron donation.
generation.uncertainty: Although trends from spectroscopic and DFT studies suggest that support-induced electronic effects are significant, the precise magnitude of the d-band center shift and its quantitative impact on adsorbate binding energies and overall catalytic performance remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two groups of catalysts with identical metal nanoparticles. Group A is deposited on a support engineered to be electron-donating, while Group B uses an electronically neutral support. Perform the same catalytic reaction (e.g., a hydrogenation or oxidation reaction) under identical conditions.
measurements: Reaction conversion rates over a fixed time period
Spectroscopic characterization (e.g., XPS, in-situ DRIFTS) to monitor shifts in the d-band center
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If catalysts on electron-donating supports do not display a statistically significant increase in turnover frequency or conversion rate compared to those on neutral supports, or if spectroscopic measurements do not show the predicted upward d-band center shift, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In conclusion, our findings reveal that the (001) facet of the P-HEO LaCr0.2Mn0.2Fe0.2Co0.2Ni0.2O3-δ is highly active for catalyzing the OER. Our study provided a one-to-one comparison of the same crystallographic facet with close to identical morphology and surface termination for a range of perovskite oxides. While the single B-site perovskites follow the OER trend expected based on the binding energy of nonbonding O 2p states, in reasonable agreement with DFT-predicted activity trends, the P-HEO electrocatalyst clearly outperforms all of its single B parent compounds. Our valence band analysis showed that the electronic structure of P-HEO is of a highly covalent nature, which is beneficial for OER activity. But the activity of P-HEO is higher than expected from electronic structure considerations. APXPS analysis showed that on adsorption of reaction intermediates several transition metals exhibit a valence change, indicating a synergistic effect in the binding of surface adsorbates, which may be the cause of the enhanced OER activity. cited_evidence.text: In this work, we proposed an unusual Sabatier principle, where the Gaussian distribution of ΔGH* with a μ value closer to 0 eV and a larger σ value on HEA catalysts could be used as the descriptor of the higher catalytic activity for HER. Theoretically, the sites with ΔGH* < μ − σ and ΔGH* > μ + σ serve as the active centers for Volmer and Tafel (or Heyrovsky) reactions (see Supplementary Fig. 4), respectively. The larger σ value indicates that the active center for the Volmer reaction has a stronger H* adsorption while the active center for Tafel (or Heyrovsky) reaction has a weaker H* adsorption (see Supplementary Fig. 5). This means that a larger σ value results in faster Volmer and Tafel (or Heyrovsky) reactions, indicating a higher catalytic activity for HER. Moreover, the symmetry of the Gaussian distribution dictates that these two active centers are guaranteed to be the strongest and the weakest, respectively, only if μ = 0 eV (see Supplementary Fig. 6). Meanwhile, other sites with moderate ΔGH* (μ - σ < ΔGH* < μ + σ) are the diffusion region (DR). The diffusion of H* on the HEA surfaces is known as H* spillover, which will be discussed in detail below.

To reveal the mechanism for the enhanced HOR performance over HEA SNWs/C, the surface properties of catalyst was studied by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurement. It is noted that all the metal elements in HEA SNWs are mixed with metal state and oxidation state. Compared to HEA NPs/C, the peak in the Pt0 4 f XPS spectrum of HEA SNWs/C positively shifts by 0.13 eV (Fig. 3a), while the peak in the Ru0 3p XPS spectrum negatively shifts by 0.36 eV (Fig. 3b), indicating that electrons might transfer from Pt to Ru in HEA SNWs. On the other hand, the Ni0 2p, Co0 2p, Fe0 2p and Mo4+ 3d XPS spectra of HEA SNWs positively shift by 0.26, 0.17, 0.93 and 0.25 eV, respectively, in comparison to HEA NPs (Supplementary Fig. 22). frame.goal: To understand and explain the mechanistic origin of catalytic performance (activity, selectivity, or durability) in transition-metal catalysts.

decision.trend: Early studies primarily relied on empirical correlations between catalyst composition, particle size, and gross structural features, while later work (e.g., the Pt/Cu single‐atom alloy study and the N–Pt/HEA catalyst study) began to focus on isolating and quantifying subtle electronic factors. Initially, improvements were achieved by alloying or creating heterogeneous structures that incidentally changed the electronic states. Over time, researchers started employing DFT and in‐situ spectroscopies to directly correlate shifts in electronic structure (such as d-band center modifications and metal–ligand interactions) with catalytic performance. However, while these experiments successfully demonstrated improved activity/selectivity/durability, they did not isolate how support or ligand-induced electronic perturbations in otherwise identical catalyst structures directly govern catalysis.
decision.unsolved: The core mechanistic link—how subtle electronic structure changes (e.g., shifts in the d-band center via support interactions or controlled doping) directly translate into improved catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability under well‐controlled conditions—remains unresolved. In particular, a controlled comparison that isolates the electronic effect from confounding factors (such as particle size or gross composition changes) is still lacking.
decision.lever: Systematically tuning the electronic state of the active metal centers by altering the support’s electronic properties (for example, by employing supports with different electron-donating or withdrawing capabilities) while holding particle size, composition, and geometric factors constant.
decision.why: This approach builds directly on the observed trends where DFT and spectroscopic evidence linked electronic structure modifications to catalytic improvements, yet did not isolate the contribution of support interactions. A controlled variable experiment would provide a rigorous testable mechanistic hypothesis by comparing catalysts with the same physical attributes but different support-induced electronic perturbations, thereby revealing if and how subtle electronic changes govern catalytic performance.
